messages.subject: Re: uneven spatial distribution of objects
messages.body_plain:
> > We wish to analyse data from wild turkey survey using distance sampling.  We
> > already have distance data for every point transect surveyed.  Those point
> > transects were placed randomly in a highly fragmented agricultural landscape.
> > We know from previous analyses that the probability of occurrence of a wild
> > turkey is correlated with the percentage of forest cover in the surveyed area.
> > Is there anyway to correct for this uneven spatial distribution of the wild
> > turkey, considering the density is higher in more forested point transect?  We
> > thought of correcting the effort according to the percentge of forest cover in

> > each point transect, is this the way to do it or is there a better way?

If all you are doing is estimating abundance (or density), then no
correction is needed.  Indeed, making a correction would generate bias in
your estimate.  If you want to model the variation in density through your
area, you could use the spatial point transect methods of chapter 4 of our
2004 book, 'advanced distance sampling'.  For that, you would need to have
data on forest cover through your region, not just at the sample points.

You could also potentially use % forest cover around a point to model
detectability, assuming that detectability is lower when there is more
forest cover.  Distance allows you to include covariates such as this.
You won't get bias in your abundance estimate however, if you do not model
this - provided the key assumptions are met.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: ANOVA and Independence
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to compare density estimates of grassland birds across
three regions. I had twelve transect lines in each region, all of
which were walked twice. Each region had a separate observer, and I
have found that I need to use separate detection functions for each
observer. I planned to make regional comparisons by inputting density
estimates given for each transect line into a 1-way ANOVA (giving me
n=12 for each region). However, I am worried that because my density
estimates within each region share a common detection function, those
estimates are not independent. If I proceed regardless, are my ANOVA
results invalid? Given that I have notable observer bias, how else can
I make these comparisons?

Thanks,
Corina Jung

Corina Jung
Division of Biology
Kansas State University
Manhattan, KS 66506
Email: cj...@ksu.edu

messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapping with covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lucas, list,

I can tell you what you need to achieve, and leave it up to you to work out
the best way to get this done.  You need to resample the points with
replacement according to your design.

So, for example, say you had 20 points randomly located in a noisy area and
another 20 in a quiet area, and your points are numbered 1-20 and 21-40.
For the first stratum, you would generate 20 pseudo-random numbers between 1
and 20 (e.g., 5, 4, 4, 19, 3, 19, etc) and for the second 20 numbers between
21 and 40.  Each of these numbers would correspond with a point and if you
sampled the number, you copy across all observations associated with that
point.  This way, you may well end up with the same data more than once
(e.g., points 4 and 19 occur twice in the above example).  There's lots of
literature available on the nonparametric bootstrap if you want to find out
more.

Another example would be if you had pairs of points (close to the noise and
far from the noise) in a sample of different industrial noise areas.  In
this case, the pair of points is the sample, so you'd randomly resample
pairs.  In each bootstrap replicate, you'd get a sample of pairs, estimate
the detection function, predict density by point, calculate difference in
density between each pair, and store the mean difference in density.  You
can then use the distribution of the mean differences over all your
bootstrap replicates to test whether the mean difference is zero, or get
confidence limits of the mean difference.

The lessons from the above are (i) you need to be clear about what the
"sample" is when designing the resampling scheme - this depends on the
design and (ii) you can use the bootstrap to estimate the distribution of
the test statistic(s) you're interested in.

On a practical note, I put some VB code on the Support page of the Distance
web site a while back.  I also have some outline R code for running the MCDS
analysis engine and harvesting results, which I wrote to incorporate in
David Borchers' wildlife population estimation simulation module WiSP.  If
anyone wants the draft R code, email me.

Cheers,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: ANOVA and Independence
messages.body_plain:
It somewhat depends on how it was done.  Did you use covariates other
than observer in the detection function? How did you handle group size?
Was it estimated by line or an average for the entire region? Most
likely you won't have a problem with independence as long as you are
scaling (using f(0)) each line in the region by a constant value and the
scalars don't overlap between regions.  You are simply adjusting the
mean regional estimates for differences in detection probability.  Think
about it this way.  Assume I had 2 groups of pigs fed two different
diets and I measured their weight after being on the diet but I used 2
different scales for the 2 groups and then found the scales weren't
accurate.  If I could obtain the correct weight with a simple constant
adjustment to each weight, the estimates themselves are still
independent, I've only adjusted their mean. If you take logarithms of
the densities they will be more normally distributed and the adjustment
for detection is additive on the log scale.  Alternatively, you can use
GLM with a Poisson distribution with over-dispersion and use effort and
f(0) by strata as an offset.

--jeff

messages.body_plain:
Hi again list!

I have to deal with repeated visits to the same point transect (exactely =
8 visits in the same season) and I've entered that number of visits as =
the survey effort.  Except, since those visits are made in the same =
season, while our birds are territorial and thus not moving very much, =
those visits are not independent.  So it is a mistake to simply divide =
the estimated density by eight.  The ideal way would be to estimate the =
density based only on the maximum number of birds detected at each =
point.  For exemple, if on the first visit only one bird was detected =
but on the second visit three birds were detected, then we can be sure =
that there were at least three birds at that point and it is simply that =
two bird were missed at the first visit.=20

Is any thing like this possible?  How can we deal with this sort of =
repeated visits, while using all our distance data in order to keep =

messages.subject: Re: repeated visits
messages.body_plain:
> > I have to deal with repeated visits to the same point transect

> > (exactely 8 visits in the same season) and I've entered that number of
> > visits as the survey effort.  Except, since those visits are made in the
> > same season, while our birds are territorial and thus not moving very
> > much, those visits are not independent.  So it is a mistake to simply
> > divide the estimated density by eight.  The ideal way would be to
> > estimate the density based only on the maximum number of birds detected
> > at each point.  For exemple, if on the first visit only one bird was
> > detected but on the second visit three birds were detected, then we can
> > be sure that there were at least three birds at that point and it is
> > simply that two bird were missed at the first visit.

It is not a mistake to do it the way you did;  the method does not assume
that the data from successive visits are independent.  This issue is
covered in the book 'introduction to distance sampling'.

> > Is any thing like this possible?  How can we deal with this sort of

> > repeated visits, while using all our distance data in order to keep

> > decent precision?

This tends to overestimate density, as by chance, even if birds only move
within their territories, you will tend to record more birds on an
occasion when by chance they are closer to your point.  If you
systematically pick out your largest count at each point, on average, you
record the birds too close to your points, and hence overestimate
densities.  (Of course, if you aren't certain of detecting a bird, even if
it is at the point, then this introduces bias in the opposite direction;
in this case, you may get lucky, and the biases may tend to cancel each
other out ...)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: pres/abs with DIST-SAMP
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am looking for some advice:
Traditionally, pres/abs was used to circumvent the underlying
detectability problem with abundances across habitats; however, I would
think that this reasoning is not really valid, and pure pres/abs can
suffer from detectabilty effects as well.

So for a predictive presence/absence model (point transects, birds), we
would like to correct survey data for detectabilities across habitats.

However, I think this leads to a catch-22 because we can correct the
'confirmed absences' for detectabilities (e.g. via EDR), but then it
results into different cut-off radii for habitats, pres and abs and
subsequently into different survey areas (=unequal spatial effort, which
is not a true comparison then across transects).

I am wondering what's the best policy for this, and are there
experiences and references on how to deal with this ?

Thanks in advance and more later

    F.

Falk Huettmann
Biology and Wildlife Dept., Institute of Arctic Biology
University of Alaska Fairbanks AK 99775-7000 USA
Email ff...@uaf.edu  Phone 907 474 7882 Fax 907 474 6716

messages.subject: Re: pres/abs with DIST-SAMP
messages.body_plain:
Dear Falk, List:

I am not sure how relevant this is to your question, (and if you already know about this, I apologize!) but the issue of teasing apart "true absence" of a species from "non-detection" during surveys has been explored in the following publications. This approach is not not based on line transects, but on capture-recapture concepts.  Mackenzie et al (2) have also developed a freeware PRESENCE to estimate the occupancy parameter.

(1). Nichols J.D. and Karanth K.U. (2002). Statistical concepts: Assessing Spatial distributions. In Monitoring Tigers and their Prey: A manual for researchers, managers and conservationists in tropical Asia (Editors: K.U. Karanth and J.D. Nichols), Centre for Wildlife Studies, Bangalore, India (Pages 29-38).  Book available from the world-wide web at Natural History Book Store, UK).

(2). MacKenzie D. I., J.D. Nichols, G. B. Lachman, S. Droege, J. A. Royle and C. Langtimm. 2002. Estimating site occupancy rates when detection probabilities are less than one. Ecology 83: 2248-2255.

(3).  Royle J. A. and Nichols J. D. 2003. Estimating abundance from repeated presence-absence data or point counts. Ecology 84: 777-790.

Best,

ULLAS KARANTH

messages.subject: Conversion from data-entry-friendly format to DISTANCE format
messages.subject_clean: Conversion from data-entry-friendly format to DISTANCE format
messages.body_plain:
In preparation for a workshop on distance sampling in a couple of weeks,
I'm converting my bird point transect data to DISTANCE format.  We
recorded birds in 25-m distance categories.  The data were entered into
MS Access in the following format, to match the data sheet for easy
entry (each of these fields separated by commas are columns in the data
table):

Site, station, visit, species, 0-25, 25-50, 50-75, 75-100, >100

Each row is a combination of site, station, visit, and species, with the
total number of detections within each distance category noted in the
appropriate column.  We also kept data separate by 3 time periods, but I
combine these time periods for most analyses.  DISTANCE requires that
each detection be its own row.  So now I'm faced with converting over
12,500 records into something like 26,000 records, entirely by hand.
Does anyone know of a way to convert a format like mine to DISTANCE
format easily?  Seems like the way I'm planning to do it could be rife
with errors and take approximately forever. I am not versed in Visual
Basic and therefore can't write a macro to do this, but I was hoping
that someone might have written one for a similar problem.  Of course I
regret not entering the data in DISTANCE format initially, but you know
what they say about hindsight.

Please direct responses to me (mdschl...@ucdavis.edu) and I will
summarize responses to the list.

Thank you!

Matt

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Dept. of Environmental Science and Policy
University of California, Davis
One Shields Avenue
Davis, CA 95616
(530) 752-2843

messages.body_plain:
A huge thanks to all who replied to my plea for assistance with this
problem (original message below).  Several people had useful advice, and
one kind soul (Aaron Ellingson of USGS) wrote a macro for me, which I
ran this morning with great success.  Aaron's program was followed by an
offer from Len Thomas to write a piece of code for me in Access, and a
detailed description from Jeremy Lindsell of a method for converting
such data without a macro.  It seems that one of the best reasons to use
distance sampling might be the generosity of its practitioners!

Aaron has agreed to allow his macro to be passed around.  Len requested
it for the DISTANCE web page, so it might end up there.  In the
meantime, I'm happy to pass it along to anyone interested.

Following my original message are the other responses I received, minus
any attachments, plus a few comments.

Matt

******************************
In preparation for a workshop on distance sampling in a couple of weeks,
I'm converting my bird point transect data to DISTANCE format.  We
recorded birds in 25-m distance categories.  The data were entered into
MS Access in the following format, to match the data sheet for easy
entry (each of these fields separated by commas are columns in the data
table):

Site, station, visit, species, 0-25, 25-50, 50-75, 75-100, >100

Each row is a combination of site, station, visit, and species, with the
total number of detections within each distance category noted in the
appropriate column.  We also kept data separate by 3 time periods, but I
combine these time periods for most analyses.  DISTANCE requires that
each detection be its own row.  So now I'm faced with converting over
12,500 records into something like 26,000 records, entirely by hand.
Does anyone know of a way to convert a format like mine to DISTANCE
format easily?
Seems like the way I'm planning to do it could be rife with errors and
take approximately forever. I am not versed in Visual Basic and
therefore can't write a macro to do this, but I was hoping that someone
might have written one for a similar problem.  Of course I regret not
entering the data in DISTANCE format initially, but you know what they
say about hindsight.

**********************************************
Hopefully, someone will tell you that Access can transpose the data.  If
not, it can be done in SAS.

You can import your Access table into SAS using PROC IMPORT

Then using PROC TRANSPOSE you should be able to transpose your data into
the proper layout so that it can be used in DISTANCE.

You'll probably have to find someone who is familiar with SAS, but it
can be done fairly easily.

Good luck,

Duane

Duane R. Diefenbach, Ph.D.
Assistant Unit Leader and
Adjunct Associate Professor of Wildlife Ecology U.S. Geological Survey
Pennsylvania Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit Pennsylvania
State University
113 Merkle Lab
University Park, PA 16802
814-865-4511
814-863-4710 (fax)
ddief...@psu.edu
http://pacfwru.cas.psu.edu

**********************************************

Hi,

I have seen these things before and elsewhere, and there are scripts and
macros that can handle that; it's like 'exploding' lines.

Your problem is the very specific original data table structure on which
the macro has to run.
Hope I am wrong, but you need a programmer to adjust that.

Best of luck and more later

   F.

Falk Huettmann
Biology and Wildlife Dept., Institute of Arctic Biology University of
Alaska Fairbanks AK 99775-7000 USA Email ff...@uaf.edu  Phone 907 474
7882 Fax 907 474 6716

**********************************************
Hi Matt, I had to do something similar to this, and was directed to this
website:
http://science.nature.nps.gov/im/monitor/protocols/birds.htm

You can have a look at the example database that is provided and with
(VERY) minimal VB skills tweak the macros in there to do what you want.

Good luck!
Lucas.

--
Lucas Habib
Graduate Student
CW405, Biological Sciences Centre
University of Alberta
Edmonton, AB T6G 2E9

Phone: (780) 492-6873

**********************************************

You could spend some time writing a program, but if I was you I'd put
the data file into Excel and copy the data 4 times into different
sheets.  Then I'd delete all the distance categories but one in each
sheet.  I'd sort it by the count in the distance column and delete all
those with 0.  Then I'd add a column with a constant value which is the
mid-point of the distance interval.  I'd rename the columns to size and
distance.  After doing that for each sheet, I'd paste them together into
a single sheet.  Should take about 2-3 hrs and will be faster than
writing a program or trying to adapt someone else's program.  You do
have one problem though in your data collection.  All you have is the
count of birds in each distance band and thus it has aggregated
different detections into one. Typically the distance is recorded to
each separate detection and the size of the group is recorded.  This
will make it difficult to determine existence of any size-bias in
detection.

--jeff=20
(Jeff Laake)

[Jeff and I subsequetntly discussed this issue regarding the recording
of group size.  I now understand that it would have been better to
record each sighting, whether it's of a single bird, a pair, or a flock,
with group size noted.  My design aggregated all sightings in all
distance categories, which we agreed was not ideal but probably not
fatal in that the vast majority of my sightings were of individual
birds.  Jeff, please correct me if I misinterpreted your comments.]

**********************************************

It is not too difficult to convert your table using a well
thought-through series of moves in Excel. A macro is not necessary if
you are only doing this a few times (once, hopefully!).
I wrote the attached instructions for a very similar data set which
should give you a clue how to do this. The main differnce to your is
that I only had two or three distance bands, but had all the points
arranged across the page, so each row was a site, species, visit
combination arranged as
follows: Site, Species, Visit, Point1_Distance1, Point1_distance2,
Point2_Distance1, Point2_Distance2, etc... up to Point10_Distance2.

The most useful new column to create is the one I've called PointMinimum
which indicates which Site_Point_species_Visit combination had any
observations at all. If there were no observations, then you only want
to keep one row relating to that combination. If there was more than one
observation, you only want to keep as many rows as there were
observations and discard any other rows with no observations in.

It should only take you about 15-20 minutes, maybe less, to do this
conversion.

Jeremy

[Jeremy Lindsell]

[Jeremy attached a description of this method as a Word document.  As I
was given a macro, I didn't attempt this version, but it does look to be
a much better method than I had been using.  With his permission, I will
gladly pass along his writeup.]

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Matthew Schlesinger

University of California, Davis
One Shields Avenue
Davis, CA 95616

messages.subject: observer error
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,
I have a large data set of point counts, and one observer who clearly
underestimated distances in his first two years of data collection.  In the
third year, we got him a laser range finder which improved his distance
estimates and now his detection function looks more like the other
observers. The data were collected in intervals so there is no way to
correct the actual distances. We would like to use his data from the first
two years and the only solution I can think of is to determine the
percentage of detections for each species that occurred in each interval in
his third year of data and then using that information calculate how many
detections should have been in each interval for the first two years of his
data collection and randomly select points to move to the next interval
category.  The data were collected at one site in Idaho on six different
250 ha units. So I could try to correct the data by species and unit (or
even by point count station, but I'm not sure there would be enough data)
by determining the percentage of points in each interval for a species in a
unit. We also have data where we sent the observer out with another
observer and they compared distance estimates, so I could use that data as
well, but again all data was collected in intervals. Any suggestions would
be appreciated.
Sincerely,
Robin Russell
reru...@fs.fed.us
